title: Competing explanations of state standing after Massachusetts v. EPA
shortTitle: Competing explanations of state standing after Massachusetts v. EPA
summary: The notes distinguish expertise, federalism, public-nuisance, and representational accounts of why states might receive special treatment.
notes:
The assigned notes present several explanations that should remain attributed. Freeman and Vermeule interpret Massachusetts as reflecting concern that political appointees displaced EPA expertise and suggest strategic use of federalism to obtain a decisive vote. The editors expressly describe that proposed account of judicial motivation as speculative.

Merrill argues, in earlier scholarship, for state attorneys general’s authority to bring public-nuisance suits, analogizing public civil enforcement to criminal prosecution; the note limits his proposal to states’ own courts. Percival responds that surrender of sovereign powers on joining the Union supplies a continuing reason to let states challenge out-of-state environmental harms despite later standing doctrines. Watts and Wildermuth distinguish proprietary, quasi-sovereign, and sovereign interests, and tie the last category to limits federal regulation places on states’ authority to govern.

The editors also consider the representative credentials of elected state attorneys general in comparison with self-appointed private public-interest plaintiffs, citing Mank. Each explanation offers a different rationale and potential scope. Later notes on rejected state suits, MOHELA, and immigration enforcement prevent the reader from treating special solicitude as a universal exemption.
